analysis.title: Brent supported by fragile flows and record freight rates
key_insights: UBS CIO raises its Brent year-end 2026 forecast to USD 110/bbl from USD 100/bbl. Spot was USD 116/bbl on 27 Oct 2026.
UBS raises its March 2027 Brent forecast to USD 95/bbl from USD 90, June 2027 to USD 90 from USD 85, and September 2027 to USD 85 from USD 80.
UBS widens the WTI discount to Brent to USD 10/bbl for December and keeps an unchanged USD 4/bbl discount for 2027.

Because the futures curve slopes downward, the December Brent forecast sits above market prices, while the 2027 forecasts are in line with or slightly below market prices. UBS keeps a moderately constructive near-term outlook.

Gulf crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz and bypass pipelines were above 17.3 mbpd in September and close to 18.8 mbpd in the first three weeks of October, versus 19.9 mbpd in January-February before the conflict (Petro-Logistics).

Higher flows have not normalized the market. At least 30 attacks on ships in and around the Strait were reported in October, the highest monthly number on record. Insurance and freight costs have risen sharply, and ship-to-ship transfers are absorbing tanker capacity.
Flows depend partly on US naval escorts, so they rely on how long the US is willing to provide that service.
Global visible oil inventories were 7.8 billion barrels at end-September, down slightly more than 500mb since February (IEA). OECD strategic stocks fell 225mb over that period.

OECD commercial inventories were down only about 38mb between February and September, so strategic releases limited the price response. With most releases now finished, UBS expects a sharper fall in commercial stocks if conditions do not improve.
Media reports suggest the risk of renewed US-Iran tension is rising, which UBS sees as an upside risk to oil prices in the near term.

Middle East to China VLCC freight rates are around USD 30-40/bbl, versus USD 1-3/bbl over the previous 10 years. Longer voyages, ship-to-ship transfers, poor vessel positioning and reduced usable tanker capacity drive this.
High freight supports Brent by improving the competitiveness of shorter-haul North Sea barrels for European buyers, and it widens the Brent-WTI spread.
Chinese crude imports fell from 12.58 mbpd in February to a low of 7.15 mbpd in June and recovered to 9.06 mbpd in September. Preliminary seaborne data suggest October could return to 10 mbpd.
Chinese crude inventories fell about 130mb between February and September (IEA), so China may be less able to cut imports and draw stocks, pointing to higher imports in coming months.
OPEC+ said in a press release that its members would engage with governments and industry to improve global shipping conditions.

sector_views.rationale: UBS expects Brent to stay elevated near USD 110/bbl at year-end on volatile Middle East supply, low inventories, record freight costs and recovering Chinese imports.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Spot sits above UBS's December forecast of USD 110/bbl, reflecting a downward-sloping futures curve.
Raised from USD 100/bbl. UBS's December forecast is above market-implied prices.
Raised from USD 90/bbl. In line with or slightly below prevailing market prices.
The December discount is widened on high freight costs.

macro_indicators.indicator: Gulf crude flows via Hormuz and bypass pipelines
macro_indicators.interpretation: Recovering from disruption but still below the 19.9 mbpd January-February average.
Recovering from a 7.15 mbpd low in June. October could reach 10 mbpd on preliminary seaborne data.
Down slightly more than 500mb since February, at multi-year lows.

macro_indicators.indicator: Middle East to China VLCC freight rate
macro_indicators.interpretation: Record level versus USD 1-3/bbl over the prior 10 years.

risk_factors: Unpredictable path of the Middle East conflict and the pace of recovery in Gulf production and global oil demand keep forecast uncertainty elevated.
Volatile Middle East loadings and flows through the Strait, with high-volume days followed by low-volume periods.
Withdrawal of US naval escorts or the cost of providing them could reduce flows.
Renewed US-Iran tension is an upside risk to oil prices.
Attacks on shipping, higher insurance and freight costs, and constrained tanker capacity.
Faster resolution of the conflict and improving conditions on the ground could limit the decline in OECD commercial inventories.
charts_described: Brent forecast chart: spot USD 116 on 27 Oct 26, forecasts USD 110 Dec 26, USD 95 Mar 27, USD 90 Jun 27, USD 85 Sep 27.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict has disrupted Gulf crude supply through the Strait of Hormuz, with Gulf loadings recovering but below pre-conflict levels.
At least 30 attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in October, the highest monthly number on record.
US naval escorts protect tankers in the Strait, and flows depend partly on how long the US keeps providing them.
Media reports suggest the risk of renewed tension between the US and Iran is rising.
OPEC+ said its members would engage with governments, industry stakeholders and international organizations to improve global shipping conditions.

tension_points.bull_case: Undersupplied market, falling commercial inventories after strategic releases end, record freight costs and recovering Chinese imports keep Brent elevated near USD 110/bbl at year-end.
tension_points.bear_case: The futures curve slopes downward and the 2027 forecasts are in line with or slightly below market prices. Gulf flows are recovering toward pre-conflict levels and the outlook is uncertain.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If conditions on the ground improve, OECD commercial inventories may not fall sharply.

theme_stances.key_argument: Volatile Middle East supply, depleted inventories, record freight and recovering Chinese imports keep Brent elevated.
theme_stances.evidence: We expect Brent crude prices to stay elevated, near USD 110/bbl

theme_stances.key_argument: Record freight costs widen the Brent-WTI spread and make shorter-haul North Sea barrels more competitive.
theme_stances.evidence: high shipping costs provide a second source of support for Brent prices
